full_judgment: 97. An argument has also been advanced by Messers Mujibur Rahman and his associates that if the application of the proviso in question does not extend to the provisions of Chapters XXXI and XXXII of the Code, with regard to appeals, revisions and references, that will lead to an anomalous situation, in view of the fact that under the provisions of the Code, as it now stands, the District Magistrate and the Additional District Magistrates have been vested with the appellate authority under sections 406, 406A and 407 and with provisional authority under sections 435, 436 and 438 of the Code in certain matters, although the Assistant Sessions Judges, who are sufficiently qualified to deal with such appeals and revision cases will be debarred from exercising such appellate and revision authority under the Code. The learned Advocates sought to argue that the Code of Criminal Procedure (Second Amendment) Ordinance 1982 (Ordinance No. XXIV of 1982), which has introduced the aforesaid proviso to section 9(3) has also amended the provision of section 407 of the Code deleting the express provision of section 407(2) of the. Code of hearing appeals by the Assistant Sessions Judges, as the legislature was well aware that no such provision needs to he kept in the Code, since in view of the proviso to section 9(3) those Assistant Sessions Judges under the deeming clause, henceforth are vested with the authority of hearing appeals, being the Additional Sessions Judges. 98. The changes in the provisions of sections 407 and 409 of the Code, sometimes allowing the Assistant Sessions Judges to hear appeals, to be preferred before the Court of Sessions or to the Sessions Judge have got a chequered history. Identical provision, as it now stands for section 407, had been in the old Code regarding hearing of appeals by the District Magistrate or any other Magistrate of First Class subordinate to him and empowered by the local government to hear such appeal on the order of conviction passed by a Magistrate Second Class or Third class of any person sentenced under section 349 by the then Sub-divisional Magistrate of Second Class. With a view to paving the way of separating the judicial and executive functions of the Magistrates in the then province of East Pakistan, now comprising Bangladesh, the then Provincial Assembly of East Pakistan on the 11th of November 1957 passed the Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Amendment) Act, 1957 and thereby omitted the provision of section 407 and substituted the original provision of section 409 of the Code as hereunder:--"409. Subject to the provisions of this section, an appeal to the Court of Sessions Judge shall be heard by the Sessions Judge or by an Additional Sessions Judge or an Assistant Sessions Judge : Provided that an Additional Sessions Judge shall hear only such appeal as the Provincial Government may, by general or special order, direct or as the Sessions Judge of the Division may make over to him Provided further that no such appeal shall be heard by an Assistant Sessions Judge unless the appeal is of a person convicted on a trial held by any Magistrate of Second class or Third class." 99. Thus, by virtue of such amendment the Assistant Sessions Judges were expressly invested with the appellate authority to hear certain appeals from the order of conviction that would be passed on a trial by the Magistrate, second class or third class. But before coming into force of such Act, under the President's Rule in the then East Pakistan, pro-claimed on the 25th June, 1958, under Article 193 of the Constitution of the then Islamic Republic of Pakistan, in exercise of the powers conferred by Article 102 of the said Constitution, the then governor on the 26th July, 1958 promulgated the Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Third Amendment) Ordinance, 1958 (East Pakistan Ordinance No LXIV of 1958); which was given effect- retrospectively with effect from the 23rd day of July, 1958, amending the provision of section 407 of the Code, substituting the words "District Magistrate" in sub-section (1) thereof by the words "Sessions Judge" and substituting the former sub-section (2) thereof making provision for the Assistant Sessions Judges to hear certain criminal appeals under the Code. The relevant provisions of that Ordinance may for information be quoted as hereunder : 2. Section 407 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, in its application to East Pakistan shall have, during the period specified in section 3, effect as if, in sub-section (1) thereof for the words "the District Magistrate", the words "Sessions Judge" were substituted and for sub-section (2) thereof the following were substituted, namely :—"(2) The Sessions Judge may direct that any appeal under sub-section (I) or any class of such appeals shall be heard by any Additional Sessions Judge or any Assistant Sessions Judge of the Sessions Division." 3. The period referred to in section 2 in respect of any area is the period beginning with the date of commencement of the Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Amendment) Ordinance, 1958, and ending with the date on which the provision of the Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Amendment) Act, 1957 is brought into force in such area. 4. Any appeal of a person convicted on a trial held by any Magistrate of the second or third class, which immediately before the commencement of the Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Amendment) Ordinance, 1958 was pending before any District Magistrate or any Magistrate subordinate to him and which stood transferred to the Sessions Judge of the Sessions Division as from the date of commencement of that Ordinance, shall be heard by him or he may transfer such appeal to such Additional Sessions Judge or such Assistant Sessions Judge, as he thinks fit, for hearing." 100. Before making such changes 'in 'section 407 there were other changes in the Code vide East Pakistan Ordinance No. XII of 1958 and the East Pakistan Ordinance No. XXXII of 1958. Later on only section 6 of the aforesaid Ordinance No. LXIV of 1958, which had repealed the Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Second Amendment) Ordinance, 1958 (East Pakistan Ordinance No XXXIII of 1958) was repealed by the East Pakistan Ordinance No. XIII of 1966. Thus, before bringing a drastic amendment, in the Code by the Code of Criminal Procedure (Second Amendment) Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. XXIV of 1982), which came into force on the 21st day of August, 1982, section 407 of the Code since 23rd July, 1958 had been in force as hereunder :—"407.—(1) Any person convicted on a trial held by any Magistrate of the Second or third class, or any person sentenced under section 349 or in respect of whom an order has been made or a sentence has been passed under section 380 by a Sub-divisional Magistrate of the second class, may appeal to Sessions Judge. (2) The Sessions Judge may direct that any appeal under sub-section (1) or any class of such appeals shall be heard by any Additional Sessions Judge or any Assistant Sessions Judge of the Sessions Division." 101. It also appears that for West Bengal, in India, the State Government of West Bengal Act 60 of 1950 amended the original provision of section 407 of the Code empowering the Sessions Judges to transfer to any Assistant Sessions Judge, subordinate to them, any appeal presented to the Court of Sessions and thereupon such Assistant Sessions Judges would hear such appeal. At present however, in India there is no provision like 407 of our Code, instead, in the original section 409 of the Code, which has been renumbered as section 381, provisions have been made to hear and dispose of certain criminal appeals by the Assistant Sessions Judge, to be preferred against conviction on a trial held by a Magistrate of the second class, under certain conditions mentioned therein. Thus, changes in the provision of section 407 of the Code might have been brought in the then Province of East Pakistan by the aforesaid Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Third Amendment) Ordinance, 1958 (East Pakistan Ordinance No. XLIV of 1958) empowering the Assistant Sessions Judges to hear and dispose of certain criminal appeals to be preferred in the Court of Session, in the light of what had earlier been brought for the State of West Bengal in India by West Bengal Act 60 of 1950. 102. It is interesting to note that in the then Province of East Pakistan, now comprising Bangladesh, although certain bold steps were taken in 1957 amending section 409 of the Code, pointed above, making provisions thereunder to hear and dispose of certain criminal appeals by the Assistant Sessions Judges by the then Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Amendment) Act 1957 (East Pakistan Act No. XXXVII of 1957) after deleting the provision of section 407 of the Code, but for obvious reasons the same was not allowed to take effect Instead the East Pakistan Ordinance No. LXIV of 1958, mentioned earlier, made the provision in section 407 empowering the Assistant Sessions Judges to hear certain criminal appeals by making amendment thereof in sub-section (2).
